chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Advance Tax Is and Why It Exists

lessons.title: Pay As You Earn: Why the Government Collects Tax Before the Year Ends

body.text: Income tax in India is not a bill you settle once a year. The law expects tax to reach the government roughly as you earn the income. For most salaried people that happens automatically through TDS. For everyone else, and for every rupee TDS misses, it happens through advance tax.

children.text: Picture two people in Pune, each owing ₹2,40,000 of income tax for the year. Meera is a salaried product manager: her employer quietly deducts tax from every monthly payslip, and she never thinks about it. Rohan is a freelance UX designer billing clients directly: nobody deducts anything, and his full fee lands in his bank account. If Rohan waits until he files his return to pay, he has used the government's money interest-free for a year, and Meera has not. The tax law does not allow that.

This lesson explains why tax is collected during the year, the two ways it happens, and why that means advance tax can apply to you even if you have a salary. Every later lesson in this course builds on this idea.
The Problem With Paying Tax Once a Year

markDefs.definition: Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, the 12-month period from 1 April to 31 March in which income is earned and taxed. It replaces the old pairing of "previous year" and "assessment year".

children.text: Your income is earned across a
tax year

running from 1 April to 31 March. The government, though, spends every single day: salaries of teachers and soldiers, interest on its borrowings, subsidies, road and rail projects. If all income tax arrived in one lump after the year closed, the Centre would have to borrow heavily for months just to keep running, and pay interest on that borrowing.

body.title: Two ways a country could collect income tax

columns.label: Pay once, after the year ends
points: Government receives nothing for 12 months or more
Taxpayers who earn early in the year hold the tax money interest-free
Big risk of people spending the money and being unable to pay later
One huge, painful payment for the taxpayer at filing time

columns.label: Pay as you earn (India's approach)
points: Tax flows in steadily through the year
Everyone pays at roughly the same pace, salaried or not
Tax is set aside before the money can be spent
The bill is spread into smaller, predictable pieces

body.text: Pay-as-you-earn is not only for the government's benefit. A freelancer who owes ₹2.4 lakh at the end of the year and has not set it aside faces a genuine cash crisis. Paying in instalments forces the saving to happen while the money is still in the account.

children.text: Two Ways Tax Is Collected During the Year

markDefs.definition: Tax deducted at source. The person paying you (an employer, bank or tenant) withholds part of the payment and deposits it with the government in your name.
Income tax you estimate and pay yourself in instalments during the tax year, on income where not enough tax has already been deducted at source.

children.text: India uses two mechanisms that work side by side. The first is
TDS
, where whoever pays you deducts tax before the money reaches you. TDS on salary is now governed by section 392 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 192 of the old 1961 Act). The second is
advance tax
, where you work out the tax yourself and pay it in instalments. The liability to pay advance tax sits in section 403 (old section 207).

markDefs.definition: Any tax still due after the tax year ends, which you pay yourself before filing your income tax return.

children.text: Whatever is still unpaid when the year ends is settled as
self-assessment tax
before you file your return. Lesson 2 shows how these three fit together on a single taxpayer's account.

body.caption: TDS vs advance tax at a glance

cells: Who works out the tax

Who deposits it
The payer, in your name and PAN
You, directly through the e-filing portal

At the time of each payment or credit
In instalments by 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March

body.title: Quick Check: TDS or Advance Tax?
body.question: Ananya works at Infosys in Bengaluru. In November she sells shares she has held for three years through her Zerodha account and makes a long-term capital gain. How is tax on that gain collected during the year?
options: Infosys deducts it through TDS on her salary
Zerodha deducts it as TDS when the sale proceeds are paid out
Ananya pays it herself as advance tax, if her total tax still due crosses the threshold
It is not taxed until she files her return, so nothing is due during the year
body.explanation: Her employer only deducts tax on salary, and brokers do not deduct TDS on capital gains of a resident individual who sells listed shares. That leaves the gain uncovered, so it falls under advance tax. Waiting until the return is filed is exactly what the law is designed to prevent.

children.text: How Much Money Moves Through Advance Tax

Advance tax is not a niche rule for a few freelancers. It is one of the largest channels through which India collects direct tax, used by every large company on NSE and BSE and by lakhs of individuals.

stats.label: Net direct tax collected, FY 2025-26
stats.context: Up 5.12% year on year, CBDT data as on 31 March 2026

stats.label: Corporate advance tax, FY 2025-26
stats.context: Up about 9.5%, after all four instalments (mid-March 2026)

stats.label: Non-corporate advance tax, FY 2025-26
stats.context: Individuals, HUFs, firms and others. Down about 1.8%

children.text: Every quarter, financial newspapers report advance tax numbers within days of each due date. Economists read them as an early signal of how corporate India's profits are tracking, well before companies publish results.
The Rule in One Line, and the Four Deadlines

body.label: When advance tax applies
body.context: If your estimated tax for the tax year, after subtracting TDS and TCS, is ₹10,000 or more, you must pay advance tax. Section 404 (old section 208). Chapter 2 covers this test and the exemptions in detail.

children.text: If you are liable, section 408 (old section 211) sets out when to pay. The due dates are cumulative: each one tells you how much of your total estimated tax must have been paid by that date, not how much to pay on that date.

body.title: Share of estimated tax that must be paid by each due date
Tax year 2026-27 from an advance taxpayer's point of view

events.title: Tax year begins
events.description: Income earned from today counts towards tax year 2026-27. Make a first rough estimate of what you will earn.

events.title: First instalment: 15%
events.description: At least 15% of your estimated tax for the year must be paid.

events.title: Second instalment: 45%
events.description: Cumulative payments must reach 45%. Revise your estimate if income has changed.

events.title: Final instalment: 100%
events.description: The full estimated tax must be paid. Taxpayers under presumptive taxation may pay everything in this single instalment instead (section 408(2)).

events.title: Tax year ends
events.description: Tax paid on or before this date still counts as advance tax for the year, though interest for the late instalment still applies.

events.title: Self-assessment tax
events.description: Any remaining balance, plus interest, is paid before the income tax return for 2026-27 is filed.

body.title: Show me the math: Rohan's four instalments

children.text: Rohan, the Pune freelancer, estimates his tax for the year at ₹2,40,000. No TDS is deducted on his fees. Here is what the cumulative schedule means in actual payments.

content.latex: \text{Payment due on a date} = (\text{Cumulative \%} \times \text{Estimated tax}) - \text{Already paid}
content.caption: Each instalment tops you up to the cumulative percentage
Instalments on an estimated tax of ₹2,40,000

cells: 15 June
15 September
15 December
15 March
Total

children.text: Notice the payments are not equal. The June payment is the smallest, and September and December carry the most weight, because 30 percentage points of the total fall due in each of those quarters.

body.title: Try It: The December Checkpoint
body.prompt: A Chennai-based marketing consultant, who does not use presumptive taxation, estimates her tax for tax year 2026-27 at ₹1,60,000, with no TDS. How much must she have paid in total by 15 December 2026? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: By 15 December, 75% of the estimated tax must have been paid cumulatively. 75% of ₹1,60,000 is ₹1,20,000. If she paid ₹24,000 in June and ₹48,000 in September (totalling ₹72,000, which is 45%), her December payment would be ₹48,000.

body.text: Missing these dates is not a criminal offence, but it is not free either. Section 424 (old section 234B) charges simple interest of 1% per month if you pay less than 90% of your tax by the end of the year, and section 425 (old section 234C) charges 1% per month for each instalment paid short or late. Chapter 4 works through both.

children.text: Why a Salaried Person Can Still Owe Advance Tax

Here is the part many salaried taxpayers miss. Your employer's TDS is calculated on your salary, and on any other income you choose to declare to payroll. It knows nothing else about you unless you tell it. Any income that TDS does not fully cover can push you over the ₹10,000 line.

body.caption: Common incomes that TDS leaves partly or fully uncovered

cells: Capital gains on shares and equity funds
Selling Nifty 50 stocks or equity mutual fund units through Zerodha or Groww
No TDS on capital gains for resident individuals
Rent from a flat
Letting out a flat in Hyderabad at ₹30,000 a month
An individual tenant only deducts TDS above ₹50,000 a month
FD and savings interest
Interest from bank FDs above the TDS threshold
TDS is 10% but your slab may be 20% or 30%
Freelance or consulting fees
Weekend design or coding work for clients
Individual clients rarely deduct TDS; business clients deduct at lower rates than your slab
Futures and options trading
Profitable F&O trades on NSE
Treated as business income, with no TDS at all

children.text: Back to Ananya. Her long-term capital gain on shares is ₹3,25,000. The first ₹1,25,000 of such gains in a year is exempt, and the rest is taxed at 12.5% plus 4% cess.

body.caption: Tax on Ananya's long-term capital gain, in rupees

children.text: That ₹26,000 is over the ₹10,000 threshold and not covered by TDS on her salary. So Ananya, a fully salaried employee, is an advance taxpayer this year. Because the gain came in November, Chapter 3 shows how instalments already past are handled.

body.title: Scenario: The Flat in Gachibowli
body.scenario: Kabir is a salaried engineering manager in Hyderabad on the new tax regime. His salary is high enough that his income is taxed at the top 30% slab, and his employer deducts TDS on it correctly every month. From April 2026 he rents out a second flat in Gachibowli to a family at ₹30,000 a month. The tenants are individuals and do not deduct any TDS. Kabir has no other income.
body.prompt: Does Kabir need to pay advance tax for tax year 2026-27? If yes, roughly how much in total, and how much should he have paid by 15 September 2026?
body.modelAnswer: Yes. Annual rent is ₹3,60,000. After the 30% standard deduction allowed on rental income, taxable income from house property is ₹2,52,000. At his 30% slab plus 4% cess, that adds ₹78,624 of tax. His employer's TDS covers only his salary, and no TDS is deducted on the rent because it is below ₹50,000 a month, so this ₹78,624 is uncovered. It is well above ₹10,000, so advance tax applies. By 15 September 2026 he should have paid 45% cumulatively, about ₹35,381 (about ₹11,794 by 15 June and about ₹23,587 more by 15 September). Many salaried landlords miss this and end up paying interest when they file.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Threshold
body.textWithBlank: You must pay advance tax if your estimated tax for the tax year, after reducing TDS and TCS, is ₹___ or more.
body.explanation: The threshold in section 404 (old section 208) is ₹10,000. It is measured on the tax still due after TDS and TCS, not on your total income. A salaried person with ₹30 lakh of income and fully covered TDS owes no advance tax, while a freelancer with ₹6 lakh of income may.

children.text: Check Your Own Position

body.title: Five-Minute Self-Check for This Tax Year
steps: Log in to the income tax e-filing portal with your PAN and open the Annual Information Statement (AIS)
Note every income that appears besides salary: interest, dividends, share and mutual fund sales, rent
Open Form 26AS from the portal and see how much TDS has been deducted against each of those incomes
List any income that is not in AIS at all, such as freelance fees from individuals or rent from individual tenants
Ask yourself: could the tax on these uncovered incomes reach ₹10,000 this year? If yes, keep going with this course before 15 June

body.label: Income Tax e-Filing Portal
body.description: Official portal of the Income Tax Department. View AIS and Form 26AS, and pay advance tax through the e-Pay Tax service.

cards.definition: The 1 April to 31 March period in which income is earned and taxed, under the Income-tax Act, 2025.
The principle that income tax should reach the government during the year the income is earned, not after it ends.
Tax deducted at source by the payer and deposited in your name. TDS on salary falls under section 392 (old section 192).
Tax you estimate and pay yourself in instalments during the tax year. Liability under section 403 (old section 207).
Tax still due after the year ends, paid before filing your return.
Advance tax applies only if estimated tax after TDS and TCS is ₹10,000 or more. Section 404 (old section 208).
15%, 45%, 75% and 100% of estimated tax paid by 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March. Section 408 (old section 211).

points: India collects income tax as income is earned, not in one lump after the tax year ends
TDS covers tax deducted by the payer; advance tax covers what TDS misses and is paid by you
Advance tax applies when estimated tax after TDS and TCS is ₹10,000 or more
Instalments are cumulative: 15%, 45%, 75% and 100% by 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March
Salaried people can still owe advance tax on capital gains, rent, interest, freelance income or F&O profits
Missing instalments costs simple interest of 1% per month under sections 424 and 425 (old 234B and 234C)
